content:
When the iPhone Duo launches next month, many third-party apps may not perform as well as Apple's built-in apps. There are reasons for this at the outset, though it should get better with time.

iPhone Duo app support comes in three tiers

Yesterday we shared how third-party software runs on the iPhone Duo. There are currently three levels of compatibility. Apps designed for iOS 26 and earlier will run in a mode that does not take advantage of the larger screen at all. If Apple launched the iPhone Duo today, every third-party app would look like this.

iOS 27 launches on Monday, and Apple is already accepting apps submitted against the new operating system. iPhone apps designed for iOS 27 already look more cohesive on the iPhone Duo. There is still unused screen space, but it is no longer as crude as the other compatibility mode.

Then there is the full iPhone Duo app compatibility mode. In this mode, apps can take full advantage of the iPhone Duo screen, including moving controls that would normally sit in the top toolbar over to the side.

Standard apps get the head start

If an app uses standard system controls and has no customisation of its toolbars or navigation bars, this is roughly what the iPhone Duo will look like out of the box.

However, many apps handle their toolbars and navigation bars with custom implementations. Look at the apps you use every day. If they look different from Apple's built-in apps, they have very likely made custom design choices inside the app that will not be mapped automatically.

As a result, those apps require far more work than simply targeting the iOS 27.1 SDK. So-called "automatic" compatibility essentially only applies to standard apps that follow Apple's layout conventions with no deviations.

(The soon-to-launch but not-yet-started) race for new development tools

The good news is that Apple will give developers preparation tools before the iPhone Duo ships to customers next month. The bad news is that work has not yet begun.

Apple first needs to ship a new version of Xcode and the first developer beta of iOS 27.1 before developers can test their apps. The Xcode simulator will then offer a virtual iPhone Duo to handle early support. But most developers will not get their hands on a real iPhone Duo until launch day.

As for apps that have done extensive custom layout work, software polish for the iPhone Duo is likely to be a much longer road. That is before you even get to all the special modes the iPhone Duo supports.

An attractive new audience for developers

Although the iPhone Duo is a niche product at first, it is still an iPhone, not a VR headset or some special version of a dedicated product.

With the iPhone Duo starting at $2,000, app developers can expect Duo users to be more willing to spend on the App Store. Prioritising software updates for Duo customers may simply be a no-brainer business decision.

That said, how social media apps, banking apps, and games of all kinds optimise for the iPhone Duo will be worth watching over the coming months. Do not expect everything to be ready on day one.

The iPhone Duo's iOS layout and capabilities are remarkably novel and ambitious, and we should expect that when a third-party app ships a great iPhone Duo version, it will be a rare cause for celebration — at least for the first few months.

The iPhone Duo will begin reaching customers on October 23. Pre-orders begin October 16.
